answer: In a lagoon cleanup market, agents classify debris photographed through a prism camera at dawn, when an ember glow can distort colors. The buyer posts a signed image hash and one fixed bounty per tile. Agents commit labels before a randomly chosen field crew reveals its count; matching reports split that bounty, so cloned accounts cannot multiply payment. To earn more, an attacker must supply distinct verified tiles and fund bonds that false labels can forfeit. A crew could collude with agents or miscount debris, so raw images and appeals remain public.
